title: Earth's Systems: Rock, Water and Weather
bigQuestion: What keeps Earth's rock, water and air moving, and how can we tell what they will do next?

story.title: The Winter the River Ran Backward
story.kicker: In December 1811, the ground under the Mississippi Valley began to shake, and it did not stop for months.
paragraphs: It was about two in the morning on December 16, 1811. The town of New Madrid sat on the Mississippi River in what is now Missouri, just across from the southern tip of Illinois. Most people were asleep in log cabins. Then the ground began to roll. Chimneys fell. Trees whipped back and forth. A deep roar came from the earth, like thunder that would not stop. People ran outside into the cold and did not go back in.

That was only the first shock. Two more huge earthquakes hit on January 23 and February 7, 1812, and hundreds of smaller ones came between them. Along the river, the ground cracked open. Sand and water shot up out of the cracks in fountains, leaving patches of sand that farmers can still find today. Whole stretches of riverbank slid into the water.

On February 7 the strangest thing happened. The riverbed rose in one place and sank in another. For a short time, the Mississippi appeared to flow backward. Boats were tossed upstream. Waterfalls formed where the river had been flat. In Tennessee, land dropped and filled with water, making a new lake called Reelfoot Lake. It is still there.

The shaking was felt over a huge part of the eastern United States. People far to the east reported that the ground trembled. Yet no one at the time could explain it. There was no volcano nearby. There were no mountains. The land was flat farm country, the same land that stretches up into Illinois. Why here?

Today scientists have an answer, and it is still a little surprising. Deep under the Mississippi Valley is an old, buried crack in the continent that never finished splitting apart. Stress builds there, and every few hundred years the rock lets go. The New Madrid seismic zone is why parts of southern Illinois have some of the strictest building rules for earthquakes in the Midwest. The earth is not done moving.
story.think: Earthquakes usually happen at the edges of plates. New Madrid is in the middle of one. What does that tell you about how much we still have to learn?

lessons.title: Three Kinds of Rock
lessons.mainIdea: Every rock forms in one of three ways, and each way leaves clues you can see.
reading: Pick up a rock in a Chicago park and look closely. Some rocks show tiny glittering crystals locked together. Some show flat layers, like pages in a book. Some look squeezed and folded, with bands that wave. Those looks are not random. A rock's look records how it formed.

*Igneous* rock forms when melted rock cools and hardens. Lava that cools fast at the surface makes small crystals, like basalt. Magma that cools slowly underground makes big crystals, like granite. *Sedimentary* rock forms when bits of sand, mud or shell pile up in layers and get pressed and glued together over a long time. Most of the bedrock under Illinois is sedimentary limestone and shale, laid down under shallow seas.

*Metamorphic* rock forms when heat and pressure change a rock without melting it. Limestone squeezed deep in the crust becomes marble. Shale becomes slate. The minerals rearrange and often line up in bands. Geologists read those bands the way a detective reads footprints: they tell how hot and how deep the rock once was.

words.d: rock that formed when melted rock cooled and hardened
rock made of layers of sand, mud or shell pressed and cemented together
rock changed by heat and pressure without melting

look.title: Two Rocks From the Same Stuff
look.text: A geologist hands you two gray rocks. One has big shiny crystals you can see without a lens. The other is fine and dull, with crystals too small to see. Both have the same minerals in them. Both are igneous.
look.prompt: Which one cooled slowly underground and which cooled fast at the surface? How do you know?

check.q: A rock shows flat layers with tiny bits of shell in them. How did it most likely form?
choices: Lava cooled quickly at the surface
Heat and pressure squeezed an older rock
Sediments piled up and were pressed together
check.why: Layers and bits of shell are the signs of sedimentary rock, which forms from piled-up sediment.

check.q: Why does granite have large crystals while basalt has small ones?
choices: Basalt has more minerals in it
Granite cooled slowly underground, giving crystals time to grow
check.why: Slow cooling gives crystals time to grow large; fast cooling at the surface makes small crystals.

check.q: Limestone is buried deep and heated but does not melt. What does it become?
check.why: Heat and pressure without melting make metamorphic rock; limestone becomes marble.

lessons.title: The Rock Cycle Never Ends
lessons.mainIdea: Rock is always being broken down, moved, remade and melted, so any rock can become any other kind.
reading: A boulder on a mountain looks permanent. It is not. Rain soaks into cracks and freezes, and the ice pries the rock apart. Roots push in. Wind and water carry off the pieces. This slow breaking is called *weathering*, and the carrying away is *erosion*. Give it enough time and the mountain becomes sand on a beach.

That sand does not stay a beach forever either. Buried under more layers, it gets pressed into sandstone. Pushed deeper and heated, the sandstone can turn into quartzite, a metamorphic rock. Pushed deeper still, it can melt into magma. If that magma cools, it is igneous rock again. Lift it up into a new mountain and the cycle starts over.

Scientists call this the *rock cycle*. It has no start and no end, and no single path. A sedimentary rock can be eroded straight back into sediment, skipping the melting step. The engine behind all of it is energy: heat from deep inside Earth pushes rock up and melts it, and sunlight drives the water and wind that wear it down.

The idea took a long time to accept. In the 1780s a Scottish scientist named James Hutton watched rivers carry silt to the sea and realized that mountains must be wearing away and new rock forming, slowly, all the time. If that was true, Earth had to be far older than most people then believed.

words.d: the breaking of rock into smaller pieces by water, ice, wind, plants or chemicals
the carrying away of rock pieces and soil by water, wind or ice
the never-ending set of changes that turn rock from one kind into another

look.title: Hutton Reads the Rivers
look.text: Hutton argued that the land we live on is slowly being worn away and carried by rivers to the sea, and that new land must be forming from those sediments to replace it. Otherwise, he wrote, the continents would long ago have vanished into the ocean.
look.cite: James Hutton, Theory of the Earth, 1788, paraphrased
look.prompt: What everyday observation was Hutton starting from, and what did it force him to conclude?

check.q: Which energy source drives the weathering and erosion part of the rock cycle?
choices: Sunlight, which powers wind and the water cycle
check.why: Sunlight drives the rain, rivers and wind that break rock down and carry it away.

check.q: Sandstone is pushed deep underground and gets very hot but does not melt. What comes next in the rock cycle?
choices: It becomes a metamorphic rock such as quartzite
check.why: Heat and pressure without melting change a rock into a metamorphic rock.

check.q: What did Hutton conclude from watching rivers carry silt to the sea?
choices: Earth must be very old, because the land wears away slowly and is remade
The sea is filling up and will soon be dry
check.why: Slow wearing and rebuilding of land needs enormous time, so Earth had to be far older than people thought.

lessons.title: Inside the Earth
lessons.mainIdea: Earth has layers, and the thin, cracked outer shell rides on hot rock that slowly flows.
reading: No one has ever drilled more than about 12 kilometers into Earth. That is a scratch on a planet 6,400 kilometers from surface to center. So how do we know what is inside? Earthquakes tell us. Their waves travel through the planet, bending and slowing as they pass through different materials. By timing those waves at stations around the world, scientists have mapped Earth's insides like a doctor reading an ultrasound.

The picture that came out has layers. The *crust* is the thin outer skin, about 7 kilometers thick under the oceans and about 35 kilometers thick under the continents. Below it is the *mantle*, nearly 2,900 kilometers of hot, dense rock. The mantle is solid, but over millions of years it flows very slowly, like cold tar. Below that is the core: an outer core of liquid iron and nickel, and an inner core of solid iron squeezed by enormous pressure.

The crust and the top of the mantle together form a stiff layer called the *lithosphere*. It is broken into huge pieces called tectonic plates. Heat from the core and from radioactive decay in the mantle keeps the rock below the plates slowly churning. That churning, along with plates sinking and pulling, moves the plates a few centimeters a year, about as fast as your fingernails grow.

words.d: Earth's thin, rocky outer layer
the thick layer of hot, slowly flowing rock between the crust and the core
the stiff outer shell of Earth, made of the crust and the top of the mantle, broken into plates

look.title: How Thick Is Each Layer?
look.prompt: Compare the crust to the mantle. If Earth were an apple, how thick would the crust be?

check.q: How do scientists know what Earth's deep interior is like?
choices: They have drilled to the core
They study how earthquake waves bend and slow as they pass through Earth
They look through the crust with powerful telescopes
check.why: Earthquake waves change speed and direction in different materials, which lets scientists map the layers.

check.q: Which layer is liquid?
check.why: The outer core is liquid iron and nickel; the inner core is solid because of extreme pressure.

check.q: About how fast do tectonic plates move?
check.why: Plates move a few centimeters a year, roughly the speed your fingernails grow.

lessons.title: Where Plates Meet
lessons.mainIdea: Most earthquakes, volcanoes and mountains happen where plates pull apart, push together or slide past each other.
reading: Put a world map of earthquakes next to a world map of volcanoes. The dots line up. They trace the edges of the tectonic plates. The ring of volcanoes around the Pacific Ocean, from Chile to Alaska to Japan, is so clear that people call it the Ring of Fire. Plate edges are where the action is.

There are three kinds of edges. At a *divergent boundary*, plates pull apart. Magma rises into the gap and hardens into new crust. The Mid-Atlantic Ridge is one; Iceland sits right on top of it. At a *convergent boundary*, plates push together. When ocean crust meets a continent, the heavier ocean plate sinks beneath, melts and feeds volcanoes. That is how the Andes and the Cascades formed. When two continents collide, neither sinks, and the crust crumples into mountains like the Himalayas.

At a *transform boundary*, plates grind sideways past each other. No crust is made or destroyed, but the rock sticks, stress builds and then it snaps. That snap is an earthquake. California's San Andreas Fault is a transform boundary. Illinois sits far from any plate edge, which is why the state has no volcanoes. But as New Madrid showed, being in the middle of a plate does not mean the ground never moves.

The idea of moving plates was rejected for decades. In 1912 Alfred Wegener noticed that the coasts of Africa and South America fit like puzzle pieces and that matching fossils sat on both sides. But he could not explain what moved the continents. Only in the 1960s, when scientists mapped the ocean floor and found young rock at the ridges and older rock farther out, did the evidence become too strong to ignore.

words.d: a plate edge where two plates pull apart and new crust forms
a plate edge where two plates push together, making mountains or volcanoes
a plate edge where two plates slide sideways past each other
a crack in Earth's crust where blocks of rock have moved

look.title: Wegener's Puzzle Pieces
look.text: Wegener pointed out that the eastern coast of South America and the western coast of Africa fit together closely, and that the same kinds of ancient rocks and fossils appear on both sides of the Atlantic. He argued the continents had once been joined and had drifted apart.
look.cite: Alfred Wegener, The Origin of Continents and Oceans, 1915, paraphrased
look.prompt: Wegener had good evidence but no explanation for what moved the continents. Should scientists have accepted his idea anyway? Why or why not?

check.q: Iceland sits on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge and has many volcanoes. What kind of boundary is that?
check.why: At the ridge, plates pull apart and magma rises to make new crust and volcanoes.

check.q: Why do the Himalayas have tall mountains but no volcanoes?
choices: Two continents collided and neither sank, so the crust crumpled upward
The plates there are pulling apart
The mantle is too cold there
check.why: When continents collide, neither plate sinks and melts, so the crust folds into mountains without volcanoes.

check.q: What evidence from the 1960s finally convinced scientists that plates move?
choices: Ocean-floor rock is youngest at the ridges and older farther away
check.why: Young rock at the ridges and older rock farther out showed the sea floor was spreading and carrying the plates.

lessons.title: Sun and Gravity Run the Water Cycle
lessons.mainIdea: Sunlight lifts water into the air and gravity brings it back down, over and over.
reading: After a storm, a puddle sits on the sidewalk. By the next afternoon it is gone. It did not leak into the concrete. It went up. Sunlight warmed the water, and molecule by molecule the liquid turned into invisible water vapor and drifted into the air. That is *evaporation*, and it is the water cycle's first step.

High up, the air is colder. Cold air cannot hold as much water vapor, so the vapor turns back into tiny liquid droplets on bits of dust. That is *condensation*, and a cloud is billions of those droplets. When droplets bump and merge until they are too heavy to float, gravity wins and they fall as rain or snow. That is *precipitation*.

Then gravity keeps working. Water runs downhill into streams and rivers, soaks into the ground, or collects in lakes and oceans. Plants pull water from soil and release it from their leaves, a step called transpiration. Sooner or later the sun lifts it again. The same water has been cycling for billions of years. A drop in your glass may once have been in a glacier, a dinosaur or Lake Michigan.

Notice the two engines. The sun supplies the energy to lift water up. Gravity supplies the pull to bring it down and move it across the land. Without the sun, nothing would evaporate. Without gravity, nothing would fall. Every river, cloud and raindrop is those two forces at work.

words.d: liquid water turning into water vapor, a gas
water vapor turning back into liquid droplets
water falling from clouds as rain, snow, sleet or hail

look.title: The Cold Glass
look.text: On a humid July day in Chicago you pour ice water into a glass and set it on the table. In a few minutes the outside of the glass is wet. No water leaked through the glass. The water came from somewhere else.
look.prompt: Where did the water on the outside of the glass come from, and which step of the water cycle is this?

check.q: What supplies the energy that turns puddle water into vapor?
check.why: The sun's energy warms water and lets molecules escape into the air as vapor.

check.q: Why do clouds form when moist air rises?
choices: The air gets warmer and holds more vapor
The air gets colder and vapor condenses into droplets
check.why: Rising air cools, and cold air cannot hold as much vapor, so vapor condenses into droplets on dust.

check.q: If gravity suddenly stopped, which step of the water cycle would fail first?
check.why: Gravity pulls droplets down as rain and pulls water downhill; without it, water would not fall or flow.

lessons.title: Where Earth's Water Is
lessons.mainIdea: Almost all of Earth's water is salty ocean, and most of the fresh water is frozen or underground.
reading: From space, Earth looks like a water planet. About 71 percent of its surface is ocean. But almost all of that water is salty. Only about 2.5 percent of Earth's water is fresh, and most of the fresh water is locked in ice sheets and glaciers or hidden underground. The lakes and rivers we can see hold a tiny sliver of the total.

Water that soaks into the ground fills the tiny spaces between grains of sand and cracks in rock. That is *groundwater*, and a layer of rock or sediment that holds it is an *aquifer*. Much of central Illinois drinks from the Mahomet Aquifer, an ancient buried river valley filled with sand and gravel. Pump it out faster than rain refills it and wells run dry.

Because so little water is fresh and reachable, where it sits matters enormously. Chicago pulls its water from Lake Michigan. Towns in western Illinois pump from the ground or draw from rivers. Deserts have almost none. The water cycle moves water around, but it does not spread it evenly, and that unevenness shapes where people can live.

words.d: water that fills spaces in soil and rock below the surface
a layer of rock or sediment underground that holds usable water

look.title: Earth's Water, by Where It Sits
look.prompt: Lakes and rivers hold almost nothing, yet that is where most people get water. Why?

check.q: About what share of Earth's water is fresh?
check.why: Only about 2.5 percent is fresh; about 97 percent is salty ocean.

check.q: Where is most of Earth's fresh water?
choices: In ice sheets, glaciers and underground
check.why: Most fresh water is frozen in ice or stored as groundwater, not in visible lakes and rivers.

check.q: A town pumps its aquifer faster than rain refills it. What will happen over time?
choices: The aquifer will fill with salt water from the ocean
Rain will increase to refill it
Wells will run dry as the water level drops
check.why: Groundwater refills slowly; pumping faster than it refills lowers the water table until wells fail.

lessons.title: The Ocean Moves Heat
lessons.mainIdea: Ocean currents carry heat around the planet and shape the weather and climate of land far away.
reading: The ocean is not a still bathtub. Wind drags on the surface and sets water moving in huge loops called *currents*. Near the equator, sunlight warms the surface water. Currents like the Gulf Stream carry that warm water north along the U.S. East Coast and across the Atlantic. That is one reason western Europe has milder winters than places at the same latitude in Canada.

There is a slower, deeper flow too. Near the poles, surface water gets cold and salty as sea ice forms, and cold salty water is dense. It sinks and creeps along the ocean floor toward the equator. Warm water flows in at the surface to replace it. This global loop, sometimes called the ocean conveyor belt, takes about a thousand years to go around and moves an enormous amount of heat.

Water holds heat far better than air or land does. A lake takes all summer to warm up and all fall to cool down. That is why Chicago's lakefront is a few degrees cooler on a hot June day and a bit warmer in early winter than the suburbs to the west. Multiply that effect by a whole ocean and you get the difference between a mild coast and a harsh interior.

words.d: a steady flow of ocean water moving in a set direction
how much mass is packed into a given space; denser water sinks

look.title: Franklin Charts the Gulf Stream
look.text: Benjamin Franklin learned from whaling captains that a strong warm current ran across the Atlantic, and that ships sailing against it lost days. He had its path drawn on a chart and advised mail-ship captains to steer around it.
look.cite: Benjamin Franklin, notes on the Gulf Stream, 1760s and 1780s, paraphrased
look.prompt: Franklin's evidence came from whalers, not scientists. Why did their experience count as good evidence?

check.q: What makes cold polar surface water sink?
choices: It is cold and salty, so it is denser
check.why: Cold, salty water is denser than warm water, so it sinks and drives the deep ocean flow.

check.q: Why is Chicago's lakefront cooler than the western suburbs on a hot June afternoon?
choices: The lake is still cool from winter and water changes temperature slowly
Wind never blows near the lake
The lake is at a higher elevation
check.why: Water holds heat and changes temperature slowly, so the lake stays cool into early summer and cools the nearby air.

check.q: What would likely happen to western Europe's winters if the Gulf Stream stopped?
choices: They would stay exactly the same
check.why: The Gulf Stream carries heat north; without it, less warm water would reach Europe and winters would be colder.

lessons.title: Air Masses and Fronts
lessons.mainIdea: Weather changes when big bodies of air with different temperatures and moisture push against each other.
reading: In Illinois the weather can flip in a day. A mild, humid afternoon turns into a line of thunderstorms, then a cold, clear morning. What changed is the air itself. Huge bodies of air, hundreds of kilometers across, sit over a region long enough to take on its temperature and moisture. Those bodies are *air masses*. Air from Canada is cold and dry. Air from the Gulf of Mexico is warm and wet.

Illinois sits where those air masses meet, with no mountains to block them. The boundary between two air masses is a *front*. At a cold front, dense cold air wedges under warm air and shoves it up fast. The rising warm air cools, its vapor condenses, and tall storm clouds build. Cold fronts bring short, hard storms and then cooler, clearer air.

At a warm front, warm air slides slowly up and over cold air. The clouds are flat and wide, and the rain is gentle and lasts longer. Weather maps draw cold fronts as blue lines with triangles and warm fronts as red lines with half circles. The triangles and circles point the way the front is moving, so you can read which way the weather is headed.

Air pressure matters too. Air sinks in a high-pressure area, warming and drying as it goes, so highs bring clear skies. Air rises in a low-pressure area, cooling and forming clouds, so lows bring storms. Most of Illinois's weather is lows and their fronts sweeping from west to east across the plains.

words.d: a huge body of air with about the same temperature and moisture all the way through
the boundary where two different air masses meet
the push of the weight of air on everything below it

look.title: Reading the Sky Before the Front
look.text: It is a warm, sticky May afternoon in Springfield. The wind is from the south. To the west, a wall of dark clouds is building higher and higher. The forecast says a cold front will pass by evening.
look.prompt: Predict the next twelve hours: what happens as the front passes, and what will the morning be like?

check.q: An air mass from the Gulf of Mexico reaches Illinois. What is it most likely like?
check.why: Air over the warm Gulf waters picks up heat and moisture.

check.q: Why do cold fronts bring tall storm clouds?
choices: Cold air slides gently over warm air
The cold air is very humid
Cold air shoves warm air up quickly, and the rising air cools and condenses
check.why: Dense cold air wedges under warm air and forces it up fast, building tall clouds.

check.q: A weather map shows high pressure settling over Illinois. What weather should you expect?
check.why: In a high-pressure area, air sinks and dries out, so skies are usually clear.

lessons.title: Weather Versus Climate
lessons.mainIdea: Weather is what the air does today; climate is the pattern of weather over many years in a place.
reading: A cold, snowy week in January does not tell you what Chicago is like. Neither does one heat wave. *Weather* is the state of the air right now or over a few days: temperature, wind, clouds, rain. *Climate* is the long-term pattern, usually measured over 30 years or more. Weather is your mood today. Climate is your personality.

What sets a region's climate? Latitude matters most: places near the equator get more direct sunlight all year. Distance from the ocean matters, since water evens out temperatures. Mountains block rain, leaving deserts on their far side. Prevailing winds and ocean currents matter. Elevation matters, because air is colder higher up.

Illinois has what scientists call a humid continental climate. It is far from any ocean, so summers are hot and winters are cold. Warm Gulf air brings plenty of rain, especially in spring and summer. Along Lake Michigan, the lake softens the extremes and, in winter, adds lake-effect snow when cold air crosses the warmer water and picks up moisture. Southern Illinois, closer to the Gulf, is warmer and has a longer growing season than the north.

words.d: what the air is doing over hours or days: temperature, wind, clouds, rain
the usual pattern of weather in a place over many years
how far north or south of the equator a place is

look.title: Average January Highs, Rounded
look.cite: NOAA climate normals, rounded to the nearest degree
look.prompt: Which factors from the lesson explain the differences among these four cities?

check.q: Which statement is about climate, not weather?
choices: Chicago winters are usually cold with some snow
A cold front passed this afternoon
check.why: Climate describes the usual pattern over many years; the others describe short-term weather.

check.q: Why is southern Illinois generally warmer than northern Illinois?
choices: It is closer to the equator and to warm Gulf air
It is farther from the ocean
It is higher above sea level
check.why: Lower latitude means more direct sunlight, and Gulf air reaches it more often.

check.q: Two cities are at the same latitude. One is on a coast and one is deep inland. Which is likely true?
choices: The inland city has milder winters
The coastal city has hotter summers and colder winters
The inland city has hotter summers and colder winters
check.why: Water evens out temperatures, so the coast is milder and the inland city has bigger swings.

lessons.title: Forecasting Storms and Floods
lessons.mainIdea: Forecasts work because scientists measure the atmosphere everywhere, then run the physics forward with computers.
reading: A tornado warning in Illinois can give people ten or fifteen minutes to get to a basement. A century ago it gave them nothing. What changed is measurement. Weather balloons, radar, satellites and thousands of ground stations now report temperature, pressure, wind and moisture every hour. Computers take those numbers and use the laws of physics to calculate what the air will do next.

Forecasts are honest about uncertainty. A forecaster says 40 percent chance of rain, not rain or no rain. The further ahead, the less certain, because tiny errors in the starting measurements grow. That is why a five-day forecast is useful but a three-week forecast is mostly a guess. Scientists run the model many times with slightly different starting numbers and look at how much the answers spread.

Some hazards are easier to see coming than others. Floods on big rivers like the Illinois and the Mississippi can be forecast days ahead, because rain upstream has to travel down. Tornadoes form in minutes, so radar that detects spinning air is the main warning tool. Illinois averages dozens of tornadoes a year, most in spring, which is why schools practice drills.

Forecasting is only half the job. A warning has to reach people and they have to act. Sirens, phone alerts and weather radios exist because a perfect forecast that no one hears saves no one. Every big storm, scientists study what worked and what did not, and the system gets a little better.

words.d: a prediction of future weather based on measurements and physics
an instrument that bounces radio waves off rain and hail to see where storms are and how they move
a natural event, like a tornado or flood, that can harm people or property

look.title: Two Forecasts
look.text: On Monday the forecast says 20 percent chance of rain on Friday. On Thursday the forecast for Friday says 80 percent. Nothing about Friday's weather has changed. The forecast changed.
look.prompt: Why does the Thursday forecast deserve more trust than the Monday one, even though both are about the same day?

check.q: Why do forecasts get less certain the further ahead they go?
choices: Small errors in the starting measurements grow over time
check.why: Tiny errors in today's measurements multiply as the model runs forward, so far-off forecasts spread out.

check.q: Which hazard can usually be forecast days in advance?
choices: A flood on a large river
check.why: River floods come from rain upstream that takes days to travel downriver, so they can be predicted early.

check.q: What is the main tool for warning people that a tornado is forming?
choices: Radar that detects spinning air in a storm
check.why: Tornadoes form in minutes; radar that spots rotation inside storms gives the short warning time we have.

lessons.title: Earthquakes in the Heartland
lessons.mainIdea: Illinois has no plate edge, but old buried faults can still shake the state, so scientists map the risk instead of predicting the day.
reading: Southern Illinois sits near two earthquake zones. The New Madrid seismic zone runs from Arkansas up toward Cairo, Illinois, along the Mississippi. The Wabash Valley zone lies along the Illinois-Indiana border. Both are old, buried breaks in the middle of the North American plate, left over from a time when the continent nearly tore apart. Stress from the plate's slow motion still loads them.

Earthquakes cannot be predicted to a day or even a year. No one has found a reliable signal that comes before the rock snaps. What scientists can do is measure. Networks of seismometers record every small shake. Digging trenches across faults shows sand blows and cracked layers from past quakes and how long ago they happened. From that record, geologists estimate how often big quakes come back, roughly every few hundred years at New Madrid.

That estimate is turned into hazard maps. The maps show how hard the ground is likely to shake in a given place over a given time. Engineers use them to decide how strong buildings, bridges and pipelines need to be. Southern Illinois counties use stricter building codes than northern ones because of it. Predicting the day is impossible; preparing for the shaking is not.

Earthquake size is reported on the *magnitude* scale. Each whole step up means about 32 times more energy released. A magnitude 5 rattles dishes; a 7 wrecks towns. The 1811 and 1812 New Madrid shocks are estimated at roughly magnitude 7 or a bit more. Modern seismometers, not old letters, would tell us exactly if it happened again.

words.d: an instrument that records the shaking of the ground
a number that describes how much energy an earthquake released
a map showing how likely strong shaking, flooding or another danger is in each place

look.title: A Settler Remembers the First Shock
look.text: Eliza Bryan, who lived through the earthquakes at New Madrid, later wrote that the first shock came about two in the morning on December 16, 1811, with a violent shaking and a terrible noise like distant thunder, followed by total darkness and the cries of people and animals.
look.cite: Eliza Bryan, letter describing the New Madrid earthquakes, 1816, paraphrased
look.prompt: Bryan wrote five years after the event. What can a memory like this tell scientists, and what can it not?

check.q: Why can southern Illinois have big earthquakes even though it is far from any plate edge?
choices: There is a volcano under Cairo
Old buried faults in the middle of the plate still carry stress
The Mississippi River shakes the ground
Plates from the Pacific reach that far
check.why: The New Madrid and Wabash Valley zones are ancient breaks inside the plate that still release stress.

check.q: What can scientists do about earthquakes at New Madrid?
choices: Estimate how often they return and map the shaking risk
check.why: Earthquakes cannot be predicted, but the past record lets scientists estimate frequency and map hazards.

check.q: A magnitude 6 earthquake compared with a magnitude 5 releases about how much more energy?
check.why: Each whole step on the magnitude scale means about 32 times more energy released.

review.q: Which rock type forms from magma cooling slowly underground?
review.why: Granite is igneous, with large crystals from slow cooling underground.

review.q: What is the main engine behind erosion and the water cycle?
review.why: Sunlight evaporates water and drives the wind and rain that wear rock down.

review.q: Where do most of the world's earthquakes and volcanoes happen?
review.why: Maps of quakes and volcanoes trace the edges of tectonic plates.

review.q: Cold, salty water near the poles sinks because it is
review.why: Cold and salty water is dense, so it sinks and drives deep ocean circulation.

review.q: A warm, humid air mass is pushed up sharply by a dense cold air mass. What happens?
choices: Tall storm clouds and hard rain, then cooler air
review.why: That is a cold front: fast-rising warm air builds tall clouds and quick storms.

choices: Hot summers, cold winters, plenty of rain
review.why: Illinois is humid continental: far from the ocean, so hot summers and cold winters, with Gulf moisture.

review.q: Why can river floods be forecast days ahead but tornadoes only minutes ahead?
choices: Rain upstream takes days to travel down; tornadoes form in minutes
review.why: Flood water takes time to move downstream, giving warning; tornadoes form too fast for long warnings.

review.q: How did the 1811 and 1812 New Madrid earthquakes change scientists' understanding?
choices: They showed the Mississippi always flows north
They proved earthquakes can be predicted
They showed that big earthquakes can happen inside a plate, not only at its edges
review.why: New Madrid is far from any plate edge, so it showed that old faults inside plates can produce major quakes.
